claims.text: A List<T> stores elements in order, can grow or shrink while the program runs, and gives access to an element by its zero-based index (its position in the sequence).
claims.source_hint: csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md l.20, l.40 ('stores elements in order and can grow or shrink'); language-reference/builtin-types/collections.md l.12 (access by index)

claims.text: A List<T> may hold the same value more than once; it does not reject duplicates.
claims.source_hint: System.Collections.Generic.List<T> API remarks (no uniqueness constraint); contrast with HashSet<T> remarks 'contains no duplicate elements'

claims.text: Finding an element of a List<T> by content — Contains, IndexOf, or a foreach with a condition — compares elements starting at the front, so the work grows in proportion to the number of elements, while access by position does not.
claims.source_hint: csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md l.40 (Contains/IndexOf) and l.53 TIP (O(1) vs O(n) meaning); List<T>.IndexOf API remarks (linear search)

claims.text: A Dictionary<TKey,TValue> stores key/value pairs, one value per key, and is the collection to use when each element has a lookup key such as a name, ID or code.
claims.source_hint: csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md l.20 ('a dictionary stores values that you reach by key'), l.57

claims.text: A hash-based lookup computes a hash code from the key, picks the one bucket associated with that hash code, and searches only inside that bucket; the number of buckets is increased as elements are added, so a bucket stays short and retrieval cost barely grows with the number of stored elements.
claims.source_hint: standard/collections/hashtable-and-dictionary-collection-types.md l.18, l.22, l.26 (buckets, hash search); Dictionary<TKey,TValue> API remarks (capacity increased as elements are added)

claims.text: The order in which a Dictionary<TKey,TValue> returns its entries when enumerated is not specified; insertion order is not part of its contract.
claims.source_hint: System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<TKey,TValue> API remarks: 'the order in which the items are returned is undefined'

claims.text: An object used as a key must not change in any way that affects its hash code while it is stored in the dictionary, or the entry can no longer be found.
claims.source_hint: System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<TKey,TValue> API remarks on keys ('must not change in any way that affects its hash value')

claims.text: By default a Dictionary<TKey,TValue> and a HashSet<T> compare keys with EqualityComparer<T>.Default, which uses the type's own Equals and GetHashCode; a record gets value-based Equals and GetHashCode from the compiler, a plain class inherits reference-based ones from Object.
claims.source_hint: csharp/language-reference/builtin-types/record.md (synthesized Equals/GetHashCode, value equality); Object.Equals/Object.GetHashCode API remarks (reference equality default)

claims.text: The Dictionary<TKey,TValue> indexer throws KeyNotFoundException when the requested key is not present; TryGetValue instead returns true or false and hands the value back through an out parameter.
claims.source_hint: csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md l.57, l.61 ('use TryGetValue when the key might not exist'); Dictionary<TKey,TValue>.Item[] exceptions

claims.text: Enumerable.ToDictionary walks the source sequence once and uses the key selector to produce each key; it throws ArgumentException when the selector produces the same key for two elements.
claims.source_hint: System.Linq.Enumerable.ToDictionary API remarks and exceptions (ArgumentException: keySelector produces duplicate keys)

claims.text: A HashSet<T> holds each value at most once: adding a value already present leaves the set unchanged, so the collection initializer { 2, 3, 2 } produces a set whose Count is 2.
claims.source_hint: System.Collections.Generic.HashSet<T> API remarks ('contains no duplicate elements'); HashSet<T>.Add returns false when the element is already present

claims.text: HashSet<T>.Contains answers membership through the same hash-code mechanism as a dictionary lookup, so it does not compare against every stored element.

Running `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- collections-choice` at tag stage-0 prints the three products in written order, then `product 2 is Chuột không dây`, then a line reporting two distinct ids and that 3 is present.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at tag stage-0: samples/DonHang.Samples/Program.cs l.18 (sample name) and Samples/Data/CollectionsChoice.cs l.10-27 — run it

claims.text: Choose the collection by the operation the code performs most often: walking in order favours a list, looking a single item up by key favours a dictionary, and asking only whether a value is present favours a set.
Searching a list by id, repeated once per element of another collection, is a common accidental slowness in junior code; building a dictionary once removes it.
A search that is linear in the size of one collection, performed once per element of another, costs the product of the two sizes rather than their sum.
claims.source_hint: csharp/fundamentals/statements/collections.md l.53 TIP (meaning of O(n)); List<T>.Contains API remarks (linear search, O(n) where n is Count), applied once per element of the outer collection

claims.text: List<T>.Find searches the list forward from the first element and returns the first element matching the predicate, so finding by content with it grows with the number of elements exactly as Contains and IndexOf do. (Asserted only in quiz q5, option b.)
claims.source_hint: System.Collections.Generic.List<T>.Find API remarks ('The List<T> is searched forward starting at the first element and ending at the last element')

claims.text: In the example repository at tag stage-0, DonHang.Samples is a console project whose runner registers this sample under the name collections-choice, and the Product type it uses carries an id, a name and a price, in that order.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: samples/DonHang.Samples/Program.cs l.18; Samples/Data/CollectionsChoice.cs l.3 (record Product(int Id, string Name, int PriceVnd))
